SUMMARY

Lockheed Martin Corporation(LMT+6.99%)reported record-high backlog and double-digit year-over-year growth in both sales and profit for the third quarter. Management raised full-year 2026 guidance for revenue, earnings, and cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, citing accelerated momentum in munitions production and stability in the F-35 program. The company is executing a strategy focused on mission technology roadmaps and digital transformation to compress the timeline from development to production. The company stated that demand for its defense capabilities remains supported by bipartisan priorities and international security requirements that are independent of specific budget cycles.

Operator:Good day, and welcome everyone to the Lockheed Martin Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results Conference Call. Today's call is being recorded. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one now. At this time, for opening remarks and introductions, I would like to turn the call over to Mark Kvasnak, Vice President, Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Mark Kvasnak:Thank you, Sarah, and good morning. I'd like to welcome everyone to our third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Joining me today on the call are Jim Taiclet, our Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer, and Evan Scott, our Chief Financial Officer. Statements made today that are not historical fact are considered forward-looking statements and are made pursuant to the safe harbor provisions of federal securities laws. Actual results may differ materially from those projected in the forward-looking statements. Please see Lockheed Martin's SEC filings for a description of some of the factors that may cause actual results to differ materially from those in the forward-looking statements.

We've posted slides on our website today that we plan to address during the call to supplement our comments. These slides also include information regarding non-GAAP measures that may be used in today's call. Please access our website at www.lockheedmartin.com and click on the investor relations link to view and follow the slides and see definitions and reconciliations for non-GAAP measures. With that, I'll turn the call over to Jim.

Jim Taiclet:Thank you, Mark. Good morning, everyone. Lockheed Martin delivered another quarter of strong program performance, growing both sales and profit by double digits, reflecting execution to the plan that we previously laid out for you. We generated $3 billion of free cash flow in the quarter and grew our backlog to another record, $292 billion. The momentum in our business is accelerating, giving us confidence to raise our full-year expectations for sales, earnings, and cash again this quarter. Evan will cover the specifics shortly.

These results are a product of the investments we made in recent years that are now delivering across our entire portfolio, from autonomous aircraft and next-generation air dominance to homeland missile defense, hypersonics, and the command and control that connects it all. We are innovating faster with the best technologies available, providing integrated capabilities across every domain to answer a defense sector demand that appears permanent, resulting in a business that is resilient through any budget cycle. Munitions are a major part of that story, but they are far from the only engine of our growth.

I also want to start by acknowledging the recent F-35 multi-year announcement, which cements its role as the free world's key front-line fighter for years ahead, and again, a continuing growth engine for Lockheed Martin. This agreement solidifies the path to 850 U.S. aircraft over a 10-year span, which will be further augmented by sales to our allies, achieving a total production at 156 aircraft per year for 10 years. This landmark agreement also enables sustainment and future development to be more effective and efficient for our customers. Staying ahead of the threat has always been our mission, and today, we are doing it faster than ever.

Over the last couple of quarters, I have explained how we are transforming Lockheed Martin, and this quarter proved it again as our increased speed of innovation showed up in every part of our business. At Skunk Works, the Vectis team went from first drawing to wind tunnel testing in under two months, released the first production part in eight months, and have flight demonstrations scheduled for next year. This progress gave me confidence to green-light an increase, and now we will build five Vectis aircraft with our own investment. That puts us in position to offer a proven, production-ready autonomous aircraft as our customers define their future requirements.

At MFC, our Precision Strike Missile Increment 2 went from flight tests in March and August to a $1.2 billion production contract within the same year. That compresses what has traditionally been a multi-year path from testing to production, getting a new maritime strike capability to the army sooner and allowing the value of our development work to be realized years earlier than normal. This production award further builds on the Department of War's broader investment in quadrupling PrSM production. Our space team recently completed a key solid rocket motor test for the Next Generation Interceptor program, keeping that program on track for fielding by 2030, strengthening the homeland missile defense, and advancing a program essential to the nation's future.

At RIMPAC, an exercise in the Pacific, our RMS team and Saildrone went from concept to a live-fire missile launch from an unmanned surface vessel in less than six months, putting proven weapons on a commercial autonomous platform and extending Lockheed Martin's capability onto an entirely new class of systems. This commercial mindset throughout our company is changing how we build as well. Partnerships are becoming a key part of how we move faster, and we are extending them all through our supply chain and beyond. GM Defense, for example, delivered its first PAC-3 components to us in under one month from the initial contract.

That adds capacity at a terrific supplier at a pace our traditional supply base couldn't match on its own, and in helping us deliver more interceptors sooner without an increase in our own capital investment. Last week, we announced the expansion of our Grand Prairie, Texas, manufacturing footprint to more than 735,000 sq ft. The expansion includes additional capability and capacity for automation and digital manufacturing, and will also bring on board a Hadrian highly automated production machine cell to supply components across our missile programs in a manufacturing-as-a-service contract. The discipline that gets capability to our customers faster also strengthens our business. When we shorten the path from development to production, we accelerate the economic return on that work.

When we invest ahead of requirements, we enter competitions for the next generation of programs already well-positioned. When we partner with commercial manufacturers and tech companies, we scale in a way that keeps our investment efficient as demand grows. Delivering programs faster is only part of the equation. The greater value comes from how these capabilities work together. Our platforms are central to Lockheed Martin, but they also form a foundation for the broader role we play, one that may be unmatched in the world, and that is driving interoperability and integration across platforms and domains to give our customers an advantage no single platform can provide on its own.

This role builds on decades of mission integration experience, connecting aircraft, missiles, earth and space-based sensors, and command and control into theater-level deterrence across land, sea, air, space, and cyber. It is a very deliberate plan, and the mission technology roadmaps we established several years ago and continue to evolve guide our development ahead of formal requests for proposals. We just don't wait for them anymore. We're not just building product before customers ask for it. We work alongside them to understand where their missions are headed so that we are ready with complete, proven solutions when they need them. Part of that is recognizing that our customers don't need to choose between exquisite platforms and affordable mass.

They need both integrated, so each makes the other one more effective. We can bring them together in a way few others can. Some examples. At Valiant Shield, our RMS team used our software-driven command and control system, powered by CommandIQ, and connecting long-range missiles, integrated air and missile defense, and remote targeting, drawing on commercial sector data and using AI to recommend specific target engagements. The RMS team is building on that work in Guam, where we developed an AI-enabled battle management prototype for the Guam defense system. We were selected by the Missile Defense Agency to move its missile defense modeling and simulation to the cloud.

In Australia, we were awarded an $800 million contract for the next tranche of AIR 6500, which is its joint air battle management system, demonstrating that our integration expertise is in demand from our allies as well. This is what it means to be the premier defense technology company, delivering proven platforms that work alongside autonomous systems enabled by AI and the best commercial technologies available. Lockheed Martin's depth of experience innovating and integrating these capabilities sets us apart. Speed gets capability into the field sooner, and integration makes it much more effective. Deterrence from conflict also depends on having it at scale.

Nowhere do these demands converge more than in munitions, and that is where our operating model is actually moving the fastest. Our munitions business is transforming to deliver at wartime speed and scale. That shift now extends beyond interceptors into air dominance. This quarter, we signed a framework agreement with the Department of War to accelerate production of the Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, our next-generation air dominance missile.

Known as JATM, this is the product of years of collaboration with the Air Force and the Navy and the kind of long-term commitment that takes time to show its full value and enables us to further accelerate production ahead of a multi-year contract, so there is no delay when the contract is signed. Australia has already committed to become this program's first international customer, an early sign of demand that broadens the program's long-term opportunity and strengthens the case for the capacity we are building today. Our interceptor franchises are scaling just as quickly. This quarter, we signed a seven-year contract for PAC-3, building on the seven-year THAAD contract signed earlier this year.

Together, these awards give us and our suppliers the kind of long-term visibility that makes bold investment possible, and we are putting it to work. Adding 2 million square feet, again, 2 million square feet of facilities to support production growth across eight sites over the next three years, and these are in places like our munition center in Troy, Alabama. More than half of those additions are already underway and under construction. Just as important is the workforce to match. This year alone, we are hiring and training over 3,000 new team members across MFC's sites. That is not happening by chance.

Well before this ramp-up began, we started building partnerships with local communities, technical schools, and colleges to develop the skilled talent pipeline we knew we would need. Those relationships are now helping us bring people on faster and preparing them to contribute from day one. These are skilled roles and good jobs, and they reflect the confidence that we have in the demand ahead. Scaling production also means our suppliers need to move at the same pace. This quarter, we placed new supplier contracts for both PAC-3 and THAAD, including a $4.7 billion supply contract with L3Harris for PAC-3 propulsion.

Since the quarter closed, we also awarded Boeing a contract for $14.7 billion to triple PAC-3 seeker production, and a $1.6 billion contract to Northrop Grumman for propulsion and other missile components. Beyond our largest partners, we are working with a much broader base. Nearly 750 suppliers across 42 states support THAAD alone, and we meet with our key suppliers regularly to keep the focus on their performance. That collaboration produces real results. Together with our suppliers, we are resolving longstanding production bottlenecks that will enable substantially higher deliveries going forward.

All of this is part of more than the $8 billion investment we are making through 2030 to modernize more than 20 facilities, expand our supply chain, and grow our workforce. It is one of the largest commitments to munitions production in our history, and it is designed to sustain this production pace for years to come, and we are ahead of schedule in this expansion as our MFC segment results demonstrate. The awards we win today do more than fill our production lines. They give us stability and resources to keep investing in what follows and the next generation of capabilities that are already taking shape.

Across every domain, we are turning years of research and development investment into products that are ready for the field. In Air and Missile Defense, we are extending the PAC-3 franchise to meet both the most common and the most advanced threats. Our new PAC-3 ACE will bring a high-performance, lower-cost interceptor for cruise missiles and short-range ballistic missiles. On the other end of the spectrum, just last week, we unveiled PAC-3 Edge, our offering for the Army's Future Interceptor program, which we have now been advanced to the next stage of development for.

Built on the combat-proven PAC-3 MSE, the Edge pairs a new seeker from our key component center of excellence at RMS, made in Lockheed Martin, with a multi-pulse motor to defeat hypersonic and other advanced threats at a greater range and higher altitude. Together, PAC-3 MSE, ACE, and Edge form a family of interceptors matched to every tier of the threat and a better cost to effect performance. In counter-drone and affordable mass, our MORFIUS X-Rotor can defeat more than 50 drones in a single flight and then be recovered, recharged, and reused.

Our Kodiak Containerized Launcher completed its first live-fire test less than six months after development started, and that device packs up to 12 GMLRS rockets into a single container that can be deployed from air, land, or sea and is highly mobile. In autonomy and AI, Skunk Works and the Air Force Test Pilot School flew the X-62 VISTA, an F-16 modified, through 27 AI-controlled intercepts across eight flights with an AI agent using live data from our Legion sensor pod to intercept a real aircraft. The full integration took just three months to complete, and that moves AI from simulation into the real flight environment that pilots will face.

It builds on the foundation for the autonomy that will power aircraft like Vectis and team with crew fighters like the F-35 and F-22. Within RMS, Sikorsky completed initial flight testing of the Nomad 100, its new uncrewed aircraft, and this is under a DARPA program where our MATRIX autonomy was selected to fly on all five competing aircraft in the DARPA fly-off, including those built by other companies. That positions us as a common foundation across a growing range of platforms and not just our own, expanding our reach as uncrewed systems become fundamental mission. In hypersonics with our space segment, we are investing to move from building individual weapons to building at scale.

Our new modular payload delivery system uses technology that has already been flight tested and re-architects it into a modular family of systems, so the same airframe can be configured for doing long-range strike, for missions that need a larger payload over a shorter distance, or for missile defense with minimal changes to the system. That modular approach reduces the engineering time and cost to bring each new capability into the field. Our Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon was fielded during an exercise illustrating our ability to deliver ready now hypersonic capabilities. The breadth of our portfolio is an important differentiator that makes all this possible.

Our new key component product center develops modular sensors, data links, and seekers that can scale across our full portfolio, helping us move faster and at a lower cost and more control of our supply chain. It is built to serve the whole company, not just a single business. RMS is already developing technology for the missiles our MFC produces, for example. Increasingly, we are looking beyond our borders for the next breakthroughs. We are partnering with IBM to establish a quantum innovation hub in Switzerland, and we have dedicated $100 million of our expanded venture fund to promising companies in the U.K. and Europe, giving us early access to world-class talent and emerging technology.

Disciplined investment in research, development, and ventures are building our position in the fastest-growing parts of the defense budget, including counter-drone, autonomy, hypersonics, and the missile defense capabilities at the core of Golden Dome. All of this is happening against a dynamic budget backdrop. Uncertainty around U.S. federal funding is nothing new for our industry, and our business is built to perform through it. Fiscal 2027 opened under a continuing resolution, and the outcome of additional funding through reconciliation is still taking shape. The demand for our capabilities, though, is driven by the threat. It has bipartisan support and is not tied to any one bill or election.

The multi-year contract structure is built for this environment, and undefinitized contract actions let production start even when appropriations will take more time. Continuing resolutions affect timing and new starts, but they do not change the direction of demand. Our largest franchises address the department's most urgent priorities, from air and missile defense to air dominance, and remain essential to their mission. This quarter showed how those pieces fit together. Speed that puts capability in our customers' hands sooner, integration that connects it across every domain, munitions production scaling to meet urgent demand, and innovation that builds the franchises of the future are all coming together.

The result is capability built from the best technology that we and our partners can bring, delivered at a pace that the current geopolitical environment demands. Our business is already performing at this level today with a track record of execution and the visibility, growth, and cash generation to carry that momentum well into the future. Now I will turn the call over to Evan to go through the financials.

Evan Scott:Thanks, Jim, and good morning, everyone. As you have seen, the momentum Jim just described is clearly visible in our financial results this quarter, with a record demand converting to backlog and double-digit growth in both sales and profit. I will take you through the numbers, including our revised raised full-year outlook. I will cover our consolidated performance, cash and capital deployment, as well as backlog and key awards. Mark will brief the segments in more detail before we open the call for questions.

Third quarter sales rose 11% year-over-year to $20.7 billion, driven by higher volume across every segment, including F-35 production and sustainment at Aeronautics, MFC munitions production ramps, new radar awards at RMS, and growth on Fleet Ballistic Missile and Next Generation Interceptor at Space. Segment operating profit was $2.2 billion, with operating margin of 10.8%, driven by volume at MFC and Aeronautics, and a favorable profit adjustment in RMS upon resolution of a contracting matter. Earnings per share were $7.97 compared to $6.95 in the prior year period. The 15% year-over-year increase was primarily related to higher segment operating profit. Turning to cash from operations was $3.4 billion in the quarter and $6.9 billion year to date.

Free cash flow was $3 billion in the quarter and $5.6 billion year to date. The primary drivers this quarter were improved working capital related to customer receipts in Aeronautics on F-35, MFC, and in Space. Year to date, we have invested $1.3 billion in capital expenditures and $1.6 billion in independent research and development. The largest share of this investment is going towards munitions capacity, and it is backed by contracted demand. Seven-year agreements on PAC-3 and THAAD give us long-term volume visibility, which underpins our confidence in the return on that capital.

Beyond our own investment in capital and independent research and development, we are also working closely with suppliers and commercial partners to accelerate production across Missiles and Fire Control. Our focus is on the speed at which we deliver capability to our customers. Our capital deployment priorities remain consistent. First, we invest in the business and in the capacity and innovation that supports long-term growth. Second, we return cash to shareholders. Consistent with this, our board recently increased the quarterly dividend by $0.15-$3.60 per share, our 24th consecutive year of dividend increases. Our balance sheet remains strong, and that gives us flexibility to invest strategically.

The Ultra Maritime acquisition remains on track to close here in the fourth quarter, and we have recently cleared all regulatory approvals required to close, and we expect to fund the acquisition with cash on hand. Our cash position allows us the capacity to consider other opportunistic investments that strengthen our portfolio and provide our shareholders with long-term growth. Our ability to invest and return cash with confidence rests on the demand we are seeing, and that dynamic manifests most clearly in our backlog. We ended the quarter with a record backlog of $292 billion, up $113 billion when compared to the third quarter of 2025, and a book-to-bill of 4x.

The largest contributor in the quarter was the PAC-3 seven-year contract, which brings that multi-year contract to a total value of up to $58.6 billion. Beyond PAC-3, demand was broad-based across all four segments. Among the highlights was $4.4 billion in C-130J contracts for 34 new production aircraft serving both U.S. and international partners. We also booked awards for GMLRS, JASSM and LRASM, F-35, Black Hawk, and Fleet Ballistic Missile program. Internationally, demand continues to grow. In MFC, we are awarded a $439 million contract for production of the Army Tactical Missile System for Taiwan's HIMARS launchers. In RMS, we were selected to establish Australia's combat systems integration capability for its future Virginia-class submarines, a program that will span decades.

A backlog of this size and duration gives us substantial visibility into our future performance, with much of next year's work already under contract and in progress. That provides a strong foundation for the years ahead, regardless of how the near-term budgets unfold. Turning to our 2026 outlook. Based on performance through the third quarter, we are raising our full year 2026 guidance again this quarter. We now expect sales of between $80 billion-$82 billion, up from our previous range, representing full year growth of approximately 8% at the midpoint. This increase reflects higher volume in MFC for the munition ramps and continued strength across our portfolio as a whole.

We expect segment operating profit of between $8.575 billion and $8.675 billion, also up from the prior outlook. This reflects stronger program performance and improved execution. We now anticipate cash from operations between $10 billion and $10.2 billion, and free cash flow between $7.8 billion and $8 billion. This is the result of solid collections, improved working capital, and a benefit from continued favorability related to the IRS tax guidance we received earlier this year. Two items to keep in mind for the fourth quarter. First, our fiscal fourth quarter includes an extra week compared to the prior period last year. Second, our outlook does not yet include Ultra Maritime, which we will incorporate once the transaction closes.

This was a quarter of strong execution, record backlog, and double-digit year-over-year expansion in both sales and profit. Our robust free cash flow supports investment and growth and simultaneously returning value to shareholders, reflected in a 24th consecutive annual dividend increase, while the multi-year backlog provides clear visibility into the years ahead. Our business is built to perform through budget cycles and changes in Washington as it has many times before, and we are investing with discipline and we have confidence in the strength of our trajectory. Now, Mark will provide additional detail on the segment level performance and outlooks.

Mark Kvasnak:Thanks, Evan. Starting with Aeronautics on slide five. Third quarter sales at Aero increased 13% year-over-year, driven by higher F-35 volume and recovery of C-130 pre-contract costs that were liquidated upon the awards Evan mentioned. Segment operating profit increased 9% compared to the prior year, as the higher sales volume was partially offset by unfavorable profit adjustments on F-16 and C-130 programs. We now project Aero to deliver full year 2026 sales of $31.1 billion-$32.5 billion and profits between $2.92 billion and $2.95 billion, slightly lower than our July guidance, driven by revised contract award timing expectations for the next lots of F-35.

As we discussed in our second quarter call, the top end of our prior guidance included a bump in sales dependent on award timing for the next lot of F-35. With this revised outlook, we shift that assumption to 2027. We see Aero's full year 2026 sales growth rate in the mid-single digits, between 3% and 7% year-over-year. Moving to Missiles and Fire Control on slide six. MFC had another very strong quarter as the production ramps on munitions programs progress ahead of schedule. Sales and profit were both up 24% year-over-year in the quarter, supporting another raise to our full year outlook.

MFC's sales range is increased to between $17.25 billion and $17.45 billion, and the profit range is moved up to between $2.395 billion and $2.425 billion. MFC is on track to grow both sales and profit about 20% year-over-year in 2026. Next is Rotary and Mission Systems on slide seven. Volumes also continue to ramp at RMS. Third quarter sales in this broad portfolio were up 3% year-over-year, driven by radars and command and control programs. Segment operating profit finished up 4% year-over-year, benefiting from the favorable resolution of a contracting matter. On a full year basis, we have made slight revisions to the outlook, tightening our range for sales and raising profit.

We expect RMS 2026 sales to finish between $17.7 billion and $18 billion, growing in the low single digits year-over-year. The RMS segment operating profit outlook is increased to between $1.88 billion and $1.9 billion. Our space segment is summarized on slide eight. In the third quarter, space grew sales 4% year-over-year, driven by Next Generation Interceptor and Fleet Ballistic Missile. Profits were comparable to third quarter 2025. Our full year outlook for space has improved from our prior guidance. We increased the lower end of the sales range and raised the outlook for operating profit. We anticipate 2026 sales in our space segment will grow between 7% and 8% year-over-year to between $13.95 billion and $14.05 billion.

Full year profit expectations are increased to between $1.38 billion and $1.4 billion. To be clear, the profit outlook does not include any ULA equity earnings for the fourth quarter 2026. The takeaway is this, the growth acceleration we signaled last quarter came through. All four segments grew again in Q3, and it is this performance across the entire portfolio that fuels another raise to our full year 2026 outlook. Sales are guided higher as the strength at MFC is more than enough to overcome the shift in the assumed timing of award for the next lot of F-35s. This higher top-line outlook is converting to bottom-line returns.

Our outlook for segment operating profit is also raised again as our solid Q3 execution drives increases at three of our four segments. Sarah, let us open the call for questions.

Operator:Thank you. If you wish to ask a question, please press star then one now on your touch tone phone. You will hear an annunciator indicating you have been placed in queue. You may remove yourself from queue at any time by pressing star then one again. We ask that you limit yourself to one question. If you are using a speaker phone, please pick up the handset before pressing the numbers. Once again, if you have a question, please press star then one at this time. Your first question comes from Gavin Parsons of UBS. Your line is open.

Gavin Parsons:Thank you. Morning.

Evan Scott:Morning.

Gavin Parsons:I could sneak in two on your prepared remarks. I mean, in the first one, you mentioned multiple growth drivers outside of MFC, and obviously there is a lot of opportunity and excitement there, but was hoping you could expand on that a little to frame the multi-year growth opportunity in the other segments. Then second, in the prepared remarks on going from concept to capability in a very short timeframe. We saw a lot of those examples at AUSA, and just given Lockheed Martin is such a big organization, would love to get any more color on how you are evolving the engineering culture internally. Thank you.

Evan Scott:You bet. Yeah, thanks, Gavin. If you look across the portfolio, I mean, very critically MFC now we have laid that long-term growth framework and have stated we expect mid-teens sales CAGRs over the next five years. That backlog is very firm as we continue to work turning additional HOAs into long-term contracts. Really across the portfolio, we see similar strength, at RMS while we continue to ramp at Sikorsky. We are seeing new strength on the radar business, with key awards that are going to give us some clear line of sight to revenue growth. Space, we see a lot of strength in the national security space side.

But the key driver there remains the strategic missile defense business, driven by programs like Fleet Ballistic Missile and NGI. Over at Aeronautics, this multi-year procurement contract that we talked about gives us the long-term production stability while we continue to invest in growth in other key parts of the portfolio. You see that with some announcements in programs such as Vectis, while the Skunk Works business continues to grow as well. The key pacing item there for growth will continue to be F-35 sustainment, where we have seen some really good budget support from our customer as we have also invested in that key capability.

Jim Taiclet:It's Jim. Going on to the engineering culture, that's a really great question to explore. There's really three parts to it. One is our origination five years ago of mission technology roadmaps, which get integrated with product roadmaps or platform roadmaps. The concept of mission technology roadmap is to look at whatever systems are available today, starting with Lockheed Martin systems like the Black Hawk or the F-35 or Aegis, and then figure out if for a given mission, like air superiority or surface warfare, for the Navy, how do we take those existing systems, networks, protocols, data links and create mission capability improvements every three to six months.

Now and then you'll have a step function increase because a new platform will emerge and enter the mission set. But generally, it's going to be incremental improvements in data link capacity, firmware, integration of different supplier products like the Saildrone ships, so to speak, with our Mark 41 launcher, is one example. So a mission technology roadmap is a whole different way of thinking about product development and engineering. It basically sends a Z-axis through all of Lockheed Martin and saying, "Well, I can get a sensor from MFC that's better than the one I have from my supplier. Let's introduce that in the F-22." It's something we are doing, actually.

So those kinds of opportunities across the entire company are now capable, where it used to be really four divisions doing their own product development and hoping that it could be stitched together. The second part of this is significant investment in model-based engineering and production. We're transforming our whole production system from design to sustainment with a digital twin and digital thread that we can use digital technology to model and test new options and opportunities and improvements without having to fiddle with hardware upfront, and do as much testing and development as we can digitally before we actually start doing flight test and component testing. So that's the second one.

So yeah, mission technology roadmap's a whole different way of looking at this on a new dimension. The model-based engineering and production system that we put in place, that's what we call 1LMX, actually, internally. The third thing is increasing the R&D budget to build prototypes based on our expectations through the mission technology roadmaps before any RFI, request for information or request for proposal, comes from the government. Therefore, you have opportunities like Vectis, which we could talk more about later here.

But essentially, we know what the range payload and survivability requirements will be for CCAs, or collaborative combat aircraft, drone wingmen, and we're designing to our expectation of what that's going to be based on our experience in manned fighters, and also our ability to seamlessly connect the manned fighter to the CCA given the F-22 and F-35 fleet. So those are three ways that we're changing the engineering culture at the company.

Operator:Your next question comes from Ron Epstein of Bank of America. Your line is open.

Ron Epstein:Yeah. Hey, Jim. Thanks. Good morning, everybody.

Jim Taiclet:Good morning.

Ron Epstein:Can we talk a bit more about Vectis, and what that means for you guys, CCA, and then just part of a broader question of, what is going on in the Skunk Works, if you can give us a little bit of flavor for that as well.

Jim Taiclet:Well, we'll try some flavor. I cannot give you a lot of details, Ron, but glad you asked. Look, the way we came up with the Vectis initiative internally was basically this mission technology roadmap concept. There are two missions that Vectis is applicable to. One is air dominance or air-to-air combat, shooting down other airplanes while surviving yourself. The second mission is strike, meaning air-to-ground missions. Aircraft delivering weapons from the air to the ground, to hit targets like integrated air missile defense batteries of the adversary.

You have the air-to-air mission, the air-to-air/ground mission with aircraft, and with the advancements in autonomy and AI and the ability to tie manned and unmanned aircraft together digitally, we just have an expectation through our mission technology roadmap and our relationships with our customers on where this is all going and what those customers, the U.S. Marines, U.S. Navy, U.S. Air Force, and our allied air forces, are going to need. That is the concept of how we came up with the idea to invest, for us fairly heavily ahead of any RFI or RFP on Vectis, because we think we know what the end game looks like. The first, I guess, real opportunity for this will be twofold.

One is there is a CCA Increment 2 program that is expected to come out of the U.S. Air Force in the next couple of years. They are doing Increment 1 at the moment, and testing and doing some flights with those models, if you will. Increment 2, we anticipate, will have, again, larger payload, larger range, and larger survivability requirement that will go with that. That is our mission technology roadmap.

But the other thing we have done is given our knowledge of those two missions, we have created internally, and I have been personally involved in this a little bit, what is the optimization equation to solve for maximum air combat capability over time at the most efficient cost to the U.S. government? That is our objective. There are three parts to achieving that objective, Ron, in my mind.
